pharm: A polyfunctional alkylating agent whose aziridine (ethyleneimine) groups form covalent cross-links with DNA, disrupting nucleic acid function and inhibiting DNA replication and cell division; it is cell-cycle nonspecific and cytotoxic to rapidly dividing cells including bone marrow.
quick: Highly indication-specific; e.g., conditioning 5-10 mg/kg IV per protocol; bladder 60 mg in 30-60 mL instilled
Can cause fetal harm - contraindicated; use effective contraception
Caution; reduced excretion may increase toxicity - monitor
Avoid during cytopenias/illness; no specific direct interaction
summary: Thiotepa is a polyfunctional alkylating cytotoxic agent of the ethyleneimine (aziridine) class. It is used as a component of high-dose conditioning regimens before hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, for treatment and palliation of certain solid tumors (including bladder cancer by intravesical instillation, and breast and ovarian carcinoma), and for controlling malignant effusions by intracavitary instillation. It alkylates and cross-links DNA, killing dividing cells. It carries a boxed warning for severe, potentially fatal myelosuppression (the principal dose-limiting toxicity) and is recognized as carcinogenic, with potential to cause secondary malignancies. It is also mutagenic and embryo-fetal toxic. Dosing is highly regimen- and indication-specific and must follow the relevant protocol, with frequent blood-count monitoring and supportive care for cytopenias, mucositis, and infection.
indications: Use as part of conditioning (high-dose chemotherapy) regimens prior to allogeneic or autologous hematopoietic progenitor (stem) cell transplantation in hematologic diseases
Treatment of adenocarcinoma of the breast and of the ovary
Control of intracavitary effusions secondary to diffuse or localized neoplastic disease of serous cavities (intrapleural, intraperitoneal, intrapericardial)
Treatment of superficial papillary carcinoma of the urinary bladder (intravesical instillation)

dosage.d: Protocol-specific, commonly 5-10 mg/kg total per regimen (often divided), per the transplant protocol
dosage.n: Administer only within a defined conditioning regimen with transplant support

dosage.d: Typically 0.3-0.4 mg/kg IV at 1-4 week intervals, then maintenance per response and counts
dosage.n: Adjust to hematologic response and toxicity

dosage.d: 0.6-0.8 mg/kg instilled into the cavity (often via the tube used to drain the fluid)
dosage.n: Drain effusion first; repeat per clinical response and counts

dosage.d: 60 mg in 30-60 mL of sterile water (or saline) retained in the bladder for ~2 hours, once weekly for 4 weeks
dosage.n: Restrict fluids ~8-12 h before; reposition patient to coat bladder wall

admin: Administer under the supervision of a physician experienced in cytotoxic therapy; handle as a hazardous drug with appropriate precautions
Reconstitute and dilute per labeling; for IV use give by the route and rate specified in the protocol
For intravesical use, instill the prepared solution and have the patient retain it ~2 hours, repositioning to bathe the entire bladder wall; restrict fluid intake beforehand
For intracavitary use, instill into the drained serous cavity, often through the drainage catheter
Obtain frequent blood counts and withhold/adjust dosing for myelosuppression; provide antiemetic and supportive care
moa: Thiotepa (triethylenethiophosphoramide) is a polyfunctional alkylating agent. Under physiologic conditions its three reactive aziridine (ethyleneimine) rings open and form covalent alkyl linkages with nucleophilic sites on DNA, particularly the N-7 position of guanine. Because the molecule is polyfunctional, it can form interstrand and intrastrand DNA cross-links, which prevent strand separation, block DNA replication and transcription, and ultimately cause cell death. The action is not specific to a particular phase of the cell cycle, so both proliferating and, to a lesser extent, resting cells are affected; rapidly dividing tissues such as bone marrow and gastrointestinal/oral mucosa are especially susceptible, accounting for the dose-limiting myelosuppression and mucositis.

absolute: Concurrent use with live vaccines in immunosuppressed patients (general cytotoxic principle)
Severe pre-existing bone marrow suppression precluding the planned dose (outside a transplant rescue context)
relative: Prior or concurrent radiation or other myelosuppressive chemotherapy
monitor: Complete blood counts frequently (nadir and recovery)

preg: Thiotepa can cause fetal harm based on its mechanism (alkylating, mutagenic) and animal data; it is contraindicated in pregnancy. Females of reproductive potential should use effective contraception during and after treatment, and males with female partners of reproductive potential should use contraception, per labeling.
lact: It is not known whether thiotepa is excreted in human milk, but because of the potential for serious adverse reactions and its cytotoxic, carcinogenic nature, breastfeeding should be discontinued during treatment.
renal: Thiotepa and its metabolites are partly renally eliminated. Use with caution in renal impairment, as reduced excretion may increase exposure and toxicity; monitor renal function and blood counts and adjust as clinically indicated.
hepatic: Thiotepa is metabolized in the liver (including to the active metabolite TEPA). Use with caution in hepatic impairment and monitor hepatic function; hepatic veno-occlusive disease (sinusoidal obstruction syndrome) can occur in the high-dose transplant setting.

major: Other myelosuppressive chemotherapy and radiation - additive, potentially severe bone marrow suppression
Live attenuated vaccines - risk of disseminated infection in immunosuppressed patients; avoid
CYP3A4 inhibitors/inducers - alter conversion of thiotepa to its active metabolite, affecting efficacy and toxicity
moderate: Drugs that inhibit aldehyde dehydrogenase or alter alkylating-agent metabolism
Other nephrotoxic or hepatotoxic agents - additive organ toxicity
minor: Concomitant agents affecting urinary pH may theoretically alter intravesical activity
interactions.alcohol: No specific direct interaction; avoid during illness and cytopenias.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause myelosuppression on CBC, transaminase and bilirubin elevations, and changes in uric acid with tumor lysis.

serious: Severe, potentially fatal bone marrow suppression (boxed warning)
Hepatic veno-occlusive disease / sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (high-dose)
emergency: Signs of hepatic veno-occlusive disease (weight gain, RUQ pain, jaundice)

monitoring: Complete blood count frequently during and after therapy (nadir and recovery)
Signs and symptoms of infection during neutropenia
Uric acid/electrolytes for tumor lysis where relevant
counsel: This is a strong chemotherapy that lowers your blood counts and can lead to infection, bleeding, and anemia - keep all blood-test appointments
Report fever, chills, sore throat, unusual bruising or bleeding, or extreme tiredness right away
Mouth soreness, nausea, and skin darkening can occur; ask about medicines and mouth care to help
This medicine can harm an unborn baby and may affect future fertility - use reliable birth control as advised, and do not breastfeed during treatment
For bladder treatments, you may be asked to limit fluids beforehand and to hold the medicine in your bladder for about 2 hours
Drink fluids as advised between treatments and tell your team about all your other medicines
pk: Cytotoxic effect over days; blood-count nadir typically 1-2 weeks after dosing
Rapid distribution after IV; active metabolite TEPA formed via CYP metabolism
Parent thiotepa terminal half-life ~1.5-4 hours; active metabolite longer
Effect on marrow persists during nadir and recovery (weeks)
Refrigerate vials (2-8 C); protect from light; use reconstituted solution promptly per labeling
pearls: BOXED WARNING: severe, potentially fatal myelosuppression is the dose-limiting toxicity - frequent CBC monitoring is mandatory
Recognized CARCINOGEN - can cause secondary malignancies; mutagenic and embryo-fetal toxic, requiring contraception
Versatile routes: IV (transplant conditioning, breast/ovary), intravesical (bladder cancer), and intracavitary (malignant effusions)
High-dose conditioning use can cause hepatic veno-occlusive disease, mucositis, skin toxicity, and CNS effects
Activated to TEPA by hepatic CYP3A4/2B6 - CYP modulators can shift efficacy/toxicity
Handle and dispose of as a hazardous cytotoxic drug; give only under experienced oncology supervision
missed: Thiotepa is administered by a healthcare professional on a defined schedule, so patients do not self-dose. If a scheduled appointment/dose is missed, contact the oncology team to reschedule; doses are timed to blood counts and the treatment protocol.
overdose: There is no specific antidote. Overdose intensifies myelosuppression (severe pancytopenia), mucositis, and organ toxicity. Management is supportive: monitor blood counts closely, provide transfusions, growth factors, antimicrobials for neutropenic infection, and intensive supportive care. Hematopoietic stem cell support may be required after marrow-ablative overexposure.
